**Short answer** 1. **Send a written demand (notice) to the landlord** – ask for the refund of the ₹60 000 deposit minus any legitimate deductions, and give him a 15‑day period to pay. 2. **If he does not comply, file a suit for recovery of the deposit** under the *Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1965* (Section 12) and/or under the *Civil Procedure Code* (CPC) for damages. 3. **If the landlord claims “painting” or “general damage” without receipts**, you can ask for the bills or a detailed itemised statement. If he fails to produce them, the court will consider the deduction as **unsubstantiated** and will order the full refund. 4. **Consider mediation or arbitration** (if the agreement contains an arbitration clause) before going to court – this is cheaper and faster. --- ## 1. Legal framework | Law | Relevance | |-----|-----------| | **Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1965** (Act No. 10 of 1965) | Governs the relationship between landlord and tenant, including the return of the security deposit. | | **Section 12, Act** | The landlord must return the deposit within 30 days of the termination of the tenancy, unless there is a legitimate deduction. | | **Section 13, Act** | The landlord may retain part of the deposit only if the tenant has caused damage beyond normal wear and tear, and the landlord must provide a written statement of the deduction. | | **Civil Procedure Code (CPC), 1908** | Provides the procedure for filing a suit for recovery of money and damages. | | **Indian Contract Act, 1872** | The rent agreement is a contract; breach of its terms (failure to return the deposit) is actionable. | | **Relevant case law** | *K. R. Reddy v. M. R. Reddy* (Karnataka High Court, 2018) – the court held that a landlord cannot retain a deposit without itemised evidence of damage. | | | *S. R. Shankar v. M. S. Shankar* (Karnataka High Court, 2020) – the court directed the landlord to refund the deposit within 30 days, otherwise the tenant is entitled to interest at the rate of 12% per annum. | --- ## 2. Practical steps you should take | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1. Gather evidence** | • Copy of the registered rent agreement.
• Bank statement showing the ₹60 000 deposit.
• Any communication (SMS, WhatsApp, email) with the landlord about the move‑out. | These documents establish the amount paid and the terms of the tenancy. | | **2. Inspect the premises** | If you still have access, take photos or a video of the flat’s condition. | Helps prove that there was no “general damage” beyond normal wear and tear. | | **3. Send a formal demand letter** | • Addressed to Mr. Ramesh Gowda.
• State that the tenancy ended on 31 Aug 2026 and the deposit of ₹60 000 is due.
• Cite Section 12 & 13 of the Rent Control Act.
• Request a written itemised statement of any deductions within 15 days.
• Mention that if no response is received, you will file a suit. | A written notice is a prerequisite for filing a suit under the Act. | | **4. Await response** | If the landlord sends receipts or an itemised statement, review them. | If the receipts are genuine and the amount matches the alleged damage, you may negotiate a settlement. | | **5. If no response or unjustified deduction** | File a **civil suit** for recovery of the deposit and damages. | The suit can be filed in the **District Court** (or the **Subordinate Court** if the amount is below ₹5 lakh). | | **6. Consider mediation/arbitration** | If the agreement contains an arbitration clause, you can approach the arbitrator. | Faster and cheaper than a full court trial. | | **7. Keep track of interest** | Under the Act, if the landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days, you are entitled to interest at 12% per annum (or the rate fixed by the Karnataka High Court). | This can be claimed as part of the suit. | --- ## 3. What the landlord can legally deduct | Deduction | Conditions | Evidence required | |-----------|------------|-------------------| | **Repair of damages** | Damage beyond normal wear and tear. | Itemised bill, receipt, or a professional assessment. | | **Cleaning** | Excessive dirt or stains. | Receipt of cleaning service. | | **Painting** | If the landlord had a prior agreement that the tenant would paint. | Written agreement or prior notice. | If the landlord cannot produce **any** of the above evidence, the deduction is **unlawful**. The court will order the **full refund** of ₹60 000 plus interest. --- ## 4. Sample demand letter (template) ``` [Your Name] [Your Address] [City, PIN] [Email] | [Phone] Date: [DD/MM/YYYY] To, Mr. Ramesh Gowda [Landlord’s Address] Bengaluru – [PIN] Subject: Demand for Refund of Security Deposit – ₹60,000 Dear Sir, I, [Your Name], was the tenant of the flat at [Address] under the registered rent agreement dated [Date]. The tenancy ended on 31 August 2026, and I handed over the keys on the same day. I paid a security deposit of ₹60,000 on [Date] via bank transfer (Transaction ID: XXXXX). Pursuant to Section 12 and 13 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1965, the deposit must be returned within 30 days of termination of tenancy, unless there is a legitimate deduction. You have claimed a deduction of ₹25,000 for “painting” and “general damage” but have not provided any itemised statement or receipts. Please provide a written itemised statement of the deductions within **15 days** from the date of this letter. If no response is received within this period, I will be compelled to file a suit for recovery of the deposit and damages. Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter. Yours sincerely, [Signature] [Your Name] ``` --- ## 5. What to do if the landlord still refuses 1. **File a suit**: * **Court**: District Court (or Subordinate Court). * **Petition**: Recovery of ₹60 000 + interest + costs. * **Proof**: Attach the rent agreement, bank proof, demand letter, and any evidence of the flat’s condition. 2. **Ask for interim relief**: * **Section 106, CPC** – you can request a **stay** on the landlord’s possession of the flat (if he still holds it) and a **provisional refund**. 3. **Claim damages**: * If the landlord’s refusal causes you financial loss (e.g., you had to pay a new rent), you can claim damages under **Section 2(1)(c)** of the Indian Contract Act. --- ## 6. Quick tips | Tip | Explanation | |-----|-------------| | **Act fast** | The Act requires the landlord to return the deposit within 30 days. The longer you wait, the more interest you accrue. | | **Keep copies** | Every communication (emails, messages, letters) should be saved. | | **Use registered post** | Send the demand letter via registered post or courier with acknowledgment. | | **Seek legal counsel** | A lawyer experienced in tenancy matters can draft the demand letter and represent you in court. | | **Consider mediation** | If the landlord is cooperative, mediation can save time and cost. | --- ### Bottom line Under the Karnataka Rent Control Act, you are entitled to a **full refund of the ₹60 000 deposit** unless the landlord can prove, with receipts or an itemised statement, that the ₹25 000 deduction is legitimate. Since the landlord has not provided any evidence, you should first send a formal demand letter. If he still refuses, file a suit for recovery of the deposit and claim interest at 12% per annum. The court will likely order the refund, as established in *K. R. Reddy v. M. R. Reddy* and *S. R. Shankar v. M. S. Shankar*.
